strengths: The contribution is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General: its primary value is scalable affordance supervision, and the deliberately conventional Espresso architecture is appropriate for demonstrating utility. The dataset scale and downstream results support a slight preference for acceptance.

Affogato substantially expands the available object assets and language supervision: 150,104 objects and 750,520 query–heatmap pairs. Deriving aligned 2D and 3D supervision from the same assets is useful for both research communities.

The strongest evidence is transfer to real images. On AGD20K-Unseen, Espresso-2D achieves zero-shot KLD/SIM/NSS of 1.571/0.376/1.016, outperforming the evaluated foundation-model baselines. The controlled comparison in Table 4b also shows that Affogato pretraining improves the same architecture from 1.034/0.503/1.550 to 0.974/0.519/1.645.

The authors audit 5,000 query–heatmap pairs from 1,000 randomly selected objects with 10 domain experts, report annotation failures, and refine test annotations. This is a meaningful quality-control effort. The supplement also candidly discusses semantic errors, segmentation bias, visibility limitations, and missing scene context.

Multiple 3D baselines, cross-category evaluations, and partial-view experiments make the resource more useful than a dataset accompanied only by illustrative examples. Pretrained model identities, hardware, and several training details are provided.
weaknesses: Annotation reliability remains incompletely characterized for a benchmark contribution. Although 72.3% of audited pairs are rated good, 12.3% are only okay and 15.4% are not good. The manuscript does not report inter-annotator agreement, rating allocation, or an independent post-refinement audit. Section 3.3 describes correcting problematic test annotations, whereas Appendix B describes filtering visibility failures; final retained counts and category distributions should be clarified.

The cross-dataset interpretation in Table 2 is too strong. Relative drops between different target datasets confound generalization with dataset difficulty and annotation conventions. On the same LASO target, Affogato-trained Espresso reaches 0.067 aIoU versus 0.178 for LASO-trained Espresso. This does not negate transfer utility, but smaller relative gaps do not establish the claimed improvement in 3D robustness. A controlled Affogato-pretraining/LASO-fine-tuning comparison would provide stronger evidence.

The open-vocabulary evaluation principally holds out object categories, not affordance concepts or language compositions. Table 3 therefore supports cross-category transfer more directly than unseen-affordance understanding. The reported >450 object classes and >350 affordances are frequency-thresholded words rather than a validated semantic inventory, limiting direct comparison with prior datasets' curated category counts.

Key pipeline claims lack controlled validation. There is no ablation of multi-view voting, view count, or dataset scale, and the claimed benefit of freezing encoders is not isolated experimentally. Coverage and pairwise heatmap KL divergence measure spread and difference, not annotation correctness; they cannot by themselves establish superior heatmap quality.

Reproducibility and release documentation need improvement. Exact generation prompts, visibility-aware aggregation equations, normalization rules, and duplicate-handling procedures are missing. The abstract claims public availability but supplies no usable link in the manuscript, and redistribution/licensing arrangements for the derived Objaverse resource are not explained.

strengths: The primary contribution is a dataset and benchmark, so I assess this as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than the default Algorithms/General. The simple architecture is appropriate for demonstrating dataset utility; lack of architectural novelty is not itself a weakness.

Affogato addresses a meaningful bottleneck in affordance grounding: limited object diversity and expensive spatial annotation. Its 150,104 assets and 750,520 query–heatmap pairs substantially expand the available supervision, with corresponding 2D and 3D representations.

The annotation pipeline combines language generation, interaction-point prediction, segmentation, and multiview aggregation into a practical scalable system. The manuscript acknowledges relevant foundations, including Fun3DU, and provides pretrained model identifiers and computational requirements.

The strongest evidence of utility is the external 2D evaluation. Table 4a shows consistent zero-shot improvements over the evaluated baselines. More convincingly, the same Espresso-2D architecture improves with Affogato pretraining in Table 4b: KLD decreases from 1.034 to 0.974, SIM increases from 0.503 to 0.519, and NSS increases from 1.550 to 1.645.

The authors audit 5,000 pairs using 10 domain experts and refine problematic test annotations. The supplementary discussion of semantic errors, segmentation bias, occluded parts, and background limitations is useful and appropriately identifies practical boundaries.
weaknesses: Benchmark reliability remains insufficiently established for the central dataset contribution. The audit reports 72.3% good, 12.3% okay, and 15.4% not good, but does not report agreement between annotators, rating allocation, or a quantitative audit after correction. Only the not-good group is explicitly refined. Section 3.3 describes correcting annotations, whereas the supplement also describes filtering invisible-target cases, leaving the final test composition unclear. Independent human annotations on a representative subset would better establish spatial accuracy and residual annotation bias.

The interpretation of Table 2 overstates the evidence for improved 3D generalization. Relative drops compare performance on different target datasets, with different annotation conventions and difficulty; a smaller drop does not establish superior transferable representations. For example, PointRefer trained on Affogato obtains 0.090 aIoU on LASO versus 0.192 when trained on LASO, while Espresso obtains 0.067 versus 0.178. These results demonstrate transfer, but do not isolate the claimed benefits of scale and diversity. A fixed-target pretraining comparison and controlled data-size experiments are missing.

The open-vocabulary evidence primarily tests unseen object categories rather than unseen affordance concepts or language compositions. Table 3 holds out object categories, but does not establish separation of interaction concepts or query semantics. The fox example is illustrative rather than systematic. Additionally, Table 1 counts frequent generated words as classes and affordances, which is not directly comparable to curated semantic taxonomies and can inflate apparent conceptual diversity.

Several central pipeline claims lack direct validation. There is no controlled comparison of single-view versus multiview annotations, aggregation variants, or data scale. Coverage and pairwise KL divergence measure annotation extent and difference, not correctness: broad or inconsistent masks can increase these scores. Consequently, Figure 3d does not substantiate the claimed superiority in annotation quality over prior datasets.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite useful implementation details. The manuscript omits exact generation prompts, the mathematical aggregation and visibility-normalization rules, and important mask-selection details. The abstract announces public availability but supplies no usable link in the provided manuscript; licensing and redistribution arrangements are also unspecified. These omissions matter particularly for a dataset-centered submission. Overall, the scale and demonstrated 2D utility make acceptance plausible, but benchmark validation and the support for the main generalization claims leave a slight preference for rejection.

strengths: The central contribution is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks rather than Algorithms/General: its value lies in scalable affordance supervision and demonstrated utility, so the deliberately simple architecture is appropriate. The balance slightly favors acceptance.

Affogato substantially expands available supervision to 150,104 objects and 750,520 query–heatmap pairs. Deriving aligned 3D and 2D annotations from the same assets is useful for studying affordance grounding across modalities.

The strongest evidence is transfer to real images. Espresso-2D outperforms the listed zero-shot baselines on both AGD20K splits. Affogato pretraining also improves the same fully supervised architecture from 1.034 to 0.974 KLD and from 0.503 to 0.519 SIM (Table 4), supporting practical dataset utility.

The authors audit 5,000 pairs from 1,000 objects with domain experts and refine poor annotations for evaluation. The supplementary material provides model identifiers, computational resources, training details, partial-view experiments, and useful discussion of annotation failures.
weaknesses: Benchmark reliability needs stronger characterization. The audit reports 72.3% good, 12.3% ok, and 15.4% not good, but gives no inter-annotator agreement or post-refinement quality assessment. Section 3.3 describes correcting poor annotations, whereas Appendix B also describes filtering invisible targets; the resulting test-set size and selection effects need clarification. Coverage and pairwise heatmap divergence measure annotation extent and variation, not correctness.

The cross-dataset interpretation in Table 2 is overstated. Relative drops measured against different in-domain datasets do not establish improved transfer on a common target. For example, Affogato-trained Espresso achieves 0.067 aIoU on LASO versus 0.178 when trained on LASO. Different dataset difficulty and annotation conventions confound the reported gap comparison; a controlled 3D pretraining/fine-tuning experiment would provide stronger evidence.

Open-vocabulary evaluation primarily tests unseen object categories, not explicitly held-out affordance concepts or language compositions. Table 3 and the qualitative fox example support category transfer, but leave the broader claims about unseen interactions insufficiently tested. Object and affordance counts based on frequent words also do not directly establish distinct semantic categories.

Important causal claims lack ablations: there is no direct quantitative evaluation of multi-view aggregation against single-view annotation, no dataset scaling study, and no frozen-versus-tuned encoder comparison despite the stated empirical validation. Moreover, unaugmented Affogato pretraining yields 1.100 KLD in Table A1, worse than 1.034 without pretraining in Table 4. The demonstrated pretraining benefit therefore depends on background augmentation and should be qualified accordingly.

Reproducibility remains incomplete for a dataset-centered contribution. The public-release statement has no accompanying link in the supplied manuscript, and exact generation prompts, voting/visibility normalization rules, duplicate handling, and redistribution licensing are not specified. The appendix supplies helpful implementation details, but these remaining omissions impede reconstructing and auditing the dataset.

strengths: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, consistent with its dataset-centered claims. The main value is scalable supervision and demonstrated transfer; architectural novelty is not necessary for that contribution.

Affogato-750K substantially expands 3D affordance supervision to 750,520 query–heatmap pairs across 150,104 objects. Combining language generation, point grounding, segmentation, and multi-view aggregation provides a practical approach to an important annotation bottleneck.

The strongest evidence is transfer across architectures and modalities. On LASO unseen, pretraining improves PointRefer aIoU from 14.6 to 18.6 and Espresso-3D from 18.7 to 20.8. On AGD20K, both Espresso-2D and AffordanceNet benefit from pretraining, supporting usefulness beyond the proposed model.

The evaluation includes valuable controls: held-out-category filtering, increasing pretraining-set sizes, background augmentation, and volume-matched cross-domain analysis. Filtered pretraining retains improvements, and the scaling experiment supports additional benefit from larger datasets.

Human inspection of 5K pairs, an explicit object-instance holdout, and a stage-specific failure analysis strengthen the dataset contribution. Quantitative transfer to real AGD20K images provides meaningful evidence beyond synthetic benchmarks.
weaknesses: The human-verified benchmark needs stronger documentation. Section 3.3 assigns disjoint subsets to annotators, so the reported 84.8% success rate does not establish inter-annotator agreement. Acceptance thresholds, adjudication, and post-correction quality are unspecified. Incorrect queries are removed, but the final retained test count is unclear despite repeated claims of 5K test pairs. Correcting interaction points also does not explain how segmentation and coverage failures are repaired.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a dataset-centered contribution. Appendix A, titled 'Dataset link,' is empty. Exact generation prompts and the mathematical details of visibility handling, voting, and heatmap normalization are absent. Section 4 says the 3D visual encoder is fine-tuned, whereas Appendix B.2 says it is frozen. Source datasets and models are cited, but redistribution and licensing arrangements are not explained.

The annotation pipeline's central design claims lack quantitative validation. CoT prompting and smallest-mask selection are assessed qualitatively, and there is no controlled comparison of single-view versus multi-view annotation quality. Coverage and pairwise heatmap divergence measure spread and diversity, not correctness; independently annotated masks on a representative subset would better substantiate reliable supervision.

Claims of consistently improved performance need qualification. Espresso-3D pretraining worsens LASO MAE from 0.102 to 0.116 on seen and 0.101 to 0.122 on unseen data, while PointRefer degrades across all seen metrics. The annotation-scale explanation is not tested. No repeated-run uncertainty is reported, which particularly matters for the smaller supervised 2D gains.

The overlap analysis is useful but not conclusive: an imperfect Gemma-based filter can miss overlaps as well as over-remove samples, so filtered results are not established lower bounds. Semantic class counts also depend on generated labels without a documented synonym-normalization audit. These limitations weaken the strongest claims about category breadth and unseen-category generalization, although the transfer results still support a slight preference for acceptance.

strengths: The main contribution is best assessed as Datasets/Benchmarks, consistent with the manuscript’s emphasis. Affogato-750K substantially expands 3D affordance supervision to 750,520 annotations over 150,104 objects. Its value does not depend on introducing a novel grounding architecture.

Transfer experiments provide meaningful evidence of utility beyond the generated benchmark. In Table 2, pretraining improves LASO unseen aIoU for OpenAD (14.6 to 15.5), PointRefer (14.6 to 18.6), and Espresso-3D (18.7 to 20.8). Improvements across architectures support the dataset’s usefulness.

The 2D results demonstrate useful synthetic-to-real transfer: Espresso-2D achieves substantially better zero-shot AGD20K results than the evaluated baselines. Within-model supervised comparisons also show benefits from dataset pretraining for both Espresso-2D and AffordanceNet.

The paper includes valuable controls and diagnostics: category-filtered pretraining, data-scale experiments, human inspection of 5K pairs, explicit instance-level test separation, and a breakdown of annotation failures. These strengthen the contribution beyond a simple assembly of foundation models.
weaknesses: The reliability of the central benchmark remains insufficiently established. Section 3.3 assigns disjoint subsets to annotators, so the 84.8% acceptance rate does not measure inter-annotator agreement. Acceptance thresholds and adjudication are unspecified. Incorrect queries are removed and points corrected, but the final test-set size and treatment of faulty mask coverage are unclear. An independently annotated subset would better establish ground-truth quality and quantify bias from verifying pipeline-generated labels.

Reproducibility has material gaps. Appendix A, titled 'Dataset link,' is empty in the supplied manuscript. The exact generation prompts and mathematical details of visibility handling, multi-view voting, and heatmap normalization are not supplied. More directly, Section 4 says the Espresso-3D visual encoder is fine-tuned, whereas Appendix B.2 says it is entirely frozen. These omissions and contradictions matter for reproducing both the dataset and reported baselines.

Several central pipeline claims have only qualitative support. Figure 8 does not quantitatively establish the advantages of chain-of-thought prompting or smallest-mask selection, and there is no controlled downstream comparison of single-view versus multi-view supervision. Coverage and pairwise heatmap divergence measure spatial extent and variation, not correctness. The evidence therefore supports the utility of the resulting dataset more strongly than the claimed reliability of individual design choices.

The open-vocabulary evidence needs more careful qualification. Table 5 is a useful control, but an unaudited Gemma-based category filter can retain false negatives; imperfect predictions do not establish that the results are a lower bound. Category counts also depend on generated labels without a clearly documented synonym-normalization procedure. Strong claims about category-independent generalization and semantic breadth exceed what these measurements establish.

Claims of consistent improvement obscure mixed results. In Table 2, Espresso-3D pretraining worsens MAE on both splits, and PointRefer worsens across all reported seen-split metrics. Some supervised 2D gains are modest, with no repeated-run uncertainty reported. These qualifications do not negate the transfer results, but they limit their strength. Overall, the demonstrated dataset utility supports a slight preference for acceptance, contingent on resolving the benchmark documentation and reproducibility concerns.

strengths: I assess this primarily as a Datasets/Benchmarks contribution, consistent with its stated emphasis. Affogato-750K addresses a meaningful bottleneck: diverse, spatially grounded affordance supervision. Its 750,520 query–heatmap pairs over 150,104 objects substantially expand existing 3D resources; architectural novelty is not necessary to justify its value.

The strongest evidence is transfer across architectures and benchmarks. On LASO unseen, pretraining improves aIoU for OpenAD from 14.6 to 15.5, PointRefer from 14.6 to 18.6, and Espresso-3D from 18.7 to 20.8. These controlled comparisons support the dataset’s usefulness beyond the proposed model.

Transfer from synthetic renderings to real imagery is encouraging. Espresso-2D achieves zero-shot AGD20K unseen SIM of 37.6 versus 25.6 for the strongest listed baseline, and pretraining also benefits fully supervised Espresso-2D and AffordanceNet.

The paper provides useful supporting analyses: human inspection of 5K pairs, an explicit failure taxonomy, object-instance separation for the new test pool, held-out-category filtering, and data-scale experiments. The simple baselines, attribution of foundation models, and discussion of camera-coverage and synthetic-domain limitations are appropriate for a dataset-centered contribution.
weaknesses: The benchmark’s human verification needs stronger documentation. The 5K pairs are assigned in disjoint subsets to annotators, so the reported 84.8% acceptance rate does not establish inter-annotator agreement. Rating thresholds, independent reassessment after correction, and the final test size after removing incorrect queries are unspecified. Re-annotating interaction points also does not clearly resolve mask-boundary or coverage errors. These details matter because reliable evaluation is a central claim.

Reproducibility remains incomplete. Appendix A, titled 'Dataset link,' is empty in the supplied manuscript. The exact prompts and mathematical specification of multi-view aggregation, including visibility normalization and treatment of unobserved points, are missing. Section 4 says the Espresso-3D vision encoder is fine-tuned, whereas Appendix B.2 says it is frozen; this materially changes the training setup.

Evidence for individual annotation-pipeline choices is mostly qualitative. There is no quantitative comparison of single-view versus multi-view annotation quality, alternative mask-selection strategies, or prompting variants. Higher heatmap coverage and pairwise KL divergence establish spatial variety rather than correctness. A controlled human-quality evaluation would better substantiate the claimed reliability improvements.

The open-vocabulary conclusions require qualification. Category counts rely on generated labels without a documented normalization procedure, and the held-out-category filter is itself judged by Gemma3 without an audited recall estimate. Imperfect filtering can miss matches as well as over-remove them, so Table 5 is useful evidence but does not establish the claimed lower bound or fully rule out category exposure.

Some performance claims are broader than the results. Espresso-3D pretraining worsens LASO MAE from 0.101 to 0.122 on unseen data, and PointRefer deteriorates across the seen metrics. Table 4 compares different supervision levels rather than demonstrating Espresso under each level. Repeated-run uncertainty is absent, and scaling experiments do not specify whether optimization budgets are matched. These reservations temper claims of uniformly consistent benefits, although the cross-architecture transfer results still support acceptance.
